title: The habitable zone
summary: The range of distances where liquid water could exist, where it lies for the Sun, and what it does not promise.

steps.heading: Where water could be liquid
body: The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where liquid water could exist on a planet's surface. NASA describes it as not too hot and not too cold.
Every star has one, but where it lies depends on how big and bright the star is.

steps.heading: The Sun's zone
body: This site draws habitable zones with the method of Kopparapu et al. (2014), which works for stars from 2600 K to 7200 K.
For the Sun, the conservative zone runs from 0.95 to 1.68 au. A wider, optimistic zone runs from 0.75 to 1.77 au. Earth, at 1.00 au, is inside both.

facts.text: Kopparapu et al. (2014) estimate habitable zones for stars from 2600 K to 7200 K.

source.name: Kopparapu et al. (2014), Habitable Zones around Main-sequence Stars, ApJL 787, L29

steps.heading: In the zone is not the same as alive
body: Mars orbits at 1.52 au, inside the conservative zone, yet its average temperature is 214 K, far below freezing. Venus, at 0.72 au, is closer to the Sun than even the optimistic inner edge.
So the zone tells you where to look first. It does not tell you a planet has water, air or life.

facts.text: Mars averages 1.52 au from the Sun, inside the conservative zone, and averages 214 K.
Venus averages 0.72 au from the Sun.
